A compiler turns source code that people can read into instructions that a processor can execute. The
journey from text to machine code passes through several stages, and each stage has one clear responsibility. The
first stage is lexical analysis. The lexer reads the raw characters of a source file and groups them into tokens:
identifiers, keywords, numbers, operators, and punctuation. Whitespace and comments are discarded here because they
carry meaning for the reader but not for the machine. A typical lexer is a small state machine, and it is usually
the fastest part of the compiler because it touches every character exactly once.

The second stage is parsing. The parser takes the flat sequence of tokens and builds a tree that reflects the
grammatical structure of the program. This tree is called an abstract syntax tree, and its nodes correspond to
expressions, statements, and declarations. Building it requires the parser to know the grammar of the language:
which token sequences are legal and how they nest. Recursive descent parsers are popular because they are easy to
write by hand and easy to read. Operator precedence, which decides that multiplication binds more tightly than
addition, is expressed directly in the structure of the parsing functions.

Once the tree exists, the compiler checks that the program makes sense. This stage is called semantic analysis, or
type checking. The compiler builds a symbol table that records every name in the program and what it refers to: a
variable, a function, a type, or a namespace. It verifies that every identifier is declared before it is used, that
functions are called with the right number of arguments, and that the types of expressions are compatible with the
places where they are used. A good type checker reports errors in plain language and points at the exact source
location that caused them.

The next stage is the generation of an intermediate representation. Instead of translating the tree directly into
machine code, most compilers first lower it into a simpler form that is independent of both the source language and
the target processor. This intermediate representation is often a three-address code, in which every instruction
computes one value from at most two operands and stores it in a temporary. The advantage of this design is that
optimizations can be written once and shared by every front end and every back end.

Optimization is where compilers earn their reputation. Some optimizations are local and safe: constant folding
evaluates expressions whose values are known at compile time, and common subexpression elimination computes a value
once and reuses it. Other optimizations are global: loop-invariant code motion moves calculations out of loops when
their results do not change between iterations, and inlining replaces a function call with the body of the function
to remove the cost of the call and to expose further optimization opportunities. Every optimization must preserve the
observable behavior of the program, which is a subtle requirement when the program reads volatile memory or when
floating-point arithmetic is involved.

The final stage is code generation. The back end selects machine instructions for the target processor, allocates
registers to variables, and arranges the instructions in an order that keeps the processor's pipeline busy. Register
allocation is usually modeled as a graph coloring problem, and instruction scheduling depends on the latencies and
throughput of each instruction on the specific microarchitecture. The output is assembly text or object code, which a
linker later combines with libraries to produce an executable file.

Understanding these stages helps programmers reason about performance. A program that the optimizer cannot analyze,
for example because it relies on pointer arithmetic across module boundaries, gives the compiler little to work
with. A program written with simple control flow and small functions gives the optimizer room to inline, vectorize,
and remove work that is never needed.

Compilers also differ in when they run. An ahead-of-time compiler produces an executable before the program ever
runs, so it can spend a long time on optimization. A just-in-time compiler runs while the program is executing. It
starts by interpreting the program or by compiling it quickly with few optimizations, and it measures which
functions are hot. Only the hot functions are then recompiled with the expensive optimizations, and the running
program switches to the new code the next time it enters that function. This approach lets the compiler use
information that no ahead-of-time compiler can have, such as the concrete types of the values that actually flow
through a function in practice.

A third model is represented by tools that translate one source language into another. These transpilers reuse the
front end of a traditional compiler but stop after the intermediate representation and print readable source in the
target language. The printed program must then be processed again by the compiler of the target language. This
extra step costs time, but it lets a project move to a new language gradually while keeping the readable output
under version control, and it lets the target language's own tooling handle the final machine-specific details.

Whatever the design, the central idea is the same: each stage converts the program into a form that is closer to
the machine and less cluttered with detail that only people need. A programmer who understands the stages can
predict what the compiler will do with a given piece of code, can read its diagnostic messages with confidence,
and can tell the difference between a program that is slow because of what it computes and a program that is slow
because the compiler could not see what it means.

"""Small utilities for scheduling, caching, and text processing.

Every function in this module is pure unless the docstring says otherwise.
"""


class Interval:
    """A half-open interval [start, end) on the number line."""

    __slots__ = ("start", "end")

    def __init__(self, start, end):
        if end < start:
            raise ValueError("interval end precedes start")
        self.start = start
        self.end = end

    def overlaps(self, other):
        """Return True when the two intervals share at least one point."""
        return self.start < other.end and other.start < self.end

    def length(self):
        return self.end - self.start


def schedule_maximum(intervals):
    """Choose the largest subset of intervals in which no two overlap.

    The classic greedy algorithm sorts by end time and repeatedly takes the
    first interval that starts at or after the end of the last one taken.
    """
    ordered = sorted(intervals, key=lambda item: (item.end, item.start))
    chosen = []
    free_at = None
    for item in ordered:
        if free_at is None or item.start >= free_at:
            chosen.append(item)
            free_at = item.end
    return chosen


class TokenBucket:
    """Allow bursts of traffic while enforcing an average rate."""

    def __init__(self, capacity, refill_per_second):
        self.capacity = float(capacity)
        self.refill = float(refill_per_second)
        self.tokens = self.capacity
        self.updated = 0.0

    def allow(self, now, cost=1.0):
        """Consume tokens at time `now`; return False when the bucket is empty."""
        elapsed = max(0.0, now - self.updated)
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + elapsed * self.refill)
        self.updated = now
        if self.tokens >= cost:
            self.tokens -= cost
            return True
        return False


def merge_sorted(left, right, key=None):
    """Merge two sorted sequences into one sorted sequence in linear time."""
    key = key or (lambda item: item)
    result = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if key(left[i]) <= key(right[j]):
            result.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result


def word_frequencies(text, stop_words=()):
    """Count words case-insensitively, ignoring punctuation and stop words."""
    counts = {}
    for raw in text.lower().split():
        word = "".join(ch for ch in raw if ch.isalnum())
        if word and word not in stop_words:
            counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1
    return counts


def longest_common_prefix(strings):
    """Return the longest prefix shared by every string in the list."""
    if not strings:
        return ""
    first = min(strings)
    last = max(strings)
    for index, character in enumerate(first):
        if character != last[index]:
            return first[:index]
    return first
